tier_reason: First-party ratio only: the root README says pure GROQ rules run via Rust/WASM '~5-10x faster' and packages/groq-wasm/README.md says '~5-10x faster than TypeScript for complex queries'; no benchmark code, workload, corpus, hardware or runtime version exists in the repo (no bench script in the groq-wasm or groq-lint package.json).

corrections.baseline: The TypeScript implementation of the GROQ lint rules in @sanity-labs/groq-lint (named as 'TypeScript' in packages/groq-wasm/README.md; also the automatic fallback when WASM is unavailable)
corrections.claimed_speedup: Root README: 'Linting: Pure GROQ rules run via Rust/WASM (~5-10x faster)'. packages/groq-wasm/README.md Performance section: 'Linting: ~5-10x faster than TypeScript for complex queries'; also 'Near-instant formatting' and 'Lower memory footprint than JavaScript AST processing' with no figures.
corrections.caveats: Ratio-only claim with no benchmark, workload, corpus, hardware, Node/browser version or sample count anywhere in the repo; neither packages/groq-wasm nor packages/groq-lint has a bench script. The WASM side wraps the third-party Rust crates atombender/groq-lint and groq-format (packages/groq-wasm/rust/src/lib.rs calls groq_lint::lint), so the speed belongs to that crate; only the 'pure GROQ' rules run in WASM, while schema-aware rules stay in TypeScript, and the two rule implementations are not shown to produce identical findings. The 5-10x range is qualified as 'for complex queries'.

notes: Claim is real but unsupported: no benchmark anywhere, only README ratios (root README and packages/groq-wasm/README.md, the latter naming TypeScript as baseline). Speed comes from wrapping atombender/groq-lint (third-party Rust) in WASM; record shortcomings: no methodology, ratio only, rule sets not shown equivalent. tier_reason: First-party README ratios from 'first tests' ('up to ~20 times faster than JS only', 'roughly 2.5 - 3 times' native time) with no table, browser, hardware, difficulty or sample count; benches/main.rs is a native-only Criterion bench of Pow::work and Pow::validate and never runs the WASM or JS solvers.

corrections.workload: Time to solve a Hashcash-style proof of work (the README says 'Hashcat'): SHA-256 over challenge plus counter until the hash has `difficulty` leading zero bits (difficulty 10-99, default 20), in the browser with the prebuilt WASM solver vs the prebuilt JS-only solver (prebuilt/browser/js/spowJs.js), and vs native Rust (src/pow.rs, sha2 crate).
corrections.caveats: The README gives ratios only ('first tests'), with no table, hardware, browser, difficulty or sample count. benches/main.rs is a native-only Criterion bench (Pow::work on five difficulty-14 challenges, Pow::validate) and the bin target (src/main.rs, 'cargo run --features server --release 20 100') prints native percentiles; neither measures WASM or JS. The JS baseline is weak: spowJs.js awaits crypto.subtle.digest('SHA-256') once per candidate and allocates a new TextEncoder each iteration, so the ~20x mostly measures per-hash async WebCrypto/promise overhead rather than JS hashing speed; a synchronous pure-JS SHA-256 loop was not compared. The wasm build is itself 2.5-3x slower than native Rust, so it beats only the JS baseline.

notes: Ratios on README confirmed verbatim; no measurement data. Main shortcoming: JS baseline awaits one async crypto.subtle.digest call per candidate hash (prebuilt/browser/js/spowJs.js), an inherently slow pattern, and the repo's Criterion bench is native-only. tier_reason: README Benchmarks tables match the record (Moon ~182,000 vs ~126,000 iter/s, '1.44x Faster', Deno bench; Sun ~319,000 vs ~577,000 ops/s Chrome and ~178,000 vs ~434,000 ops/s Deno). Bench code is public (benches/comparison.ts via 'deno task bench', benches/deno_throughput.ts, benches/browser_bench.html) but no CPU, Deno, Chrome or compiler versions are stated, so first-party C.

corrections.baseline: astronomy-engine 2.1.19 (pure-JavaScript astronomy library; version pinned in deno.json and benches/browser_bench.html)
corrections.license: MIT for the wrapper (LICENSE, Cargo.toml, deno.json), but the WASM compiles in Swiss Ephemeris 2.10.03 C sources (vendor/swisseph submodule of aloistr/swisseph), which are dual-licensed AGPL-3.0 or Swiss Ephemeris Professional License (the README calls it 'GPL/Commercial')
corrections.workload: One fixed date (2000-01-01 12:00 UT) repeated every iteration. benches/comparison.ts (deno bench): swe_julday + swe_calc_ut(SE_SUN or SE_MOON, SEFLG_SWIEPH|SEFLG_SPEED) vs astronomy-engine GeoVector(Body, new Date('2000-01-01T12:00:00Z'), aberration=true). benches/deno_throughput.ts and benches/browser_bench.html: 100,000 Sun iterations each, timed with performance.now().
corrections.caveats: One winning row (Moon, Deno bench only) against two losing rows (Sun, Chrome and Deno); no CPU, Deno or Chrome versions stated. The two libraries return different things (Swiss Ephemeris ecliptic longitude/latitude/distance with speeds vs astronomy-engine's equatorial J2000 GeoVector), so work per call differs. Per source reading (not run): the WASM build stubs fopen to return NULL (src/lib.rs), so no ephemeris files can load and SEFLG_SWIEPH silently falls back to the Moshier analytic ephemeris on every call; the README's 'high-precision'/'more accurate' claim therefore refers to Moshier, not the SE1 files, and swe_calc_ut then repeats the calculation because the returned ephemeris flag differs from the requested one (sweph.c), so the WASM side likely does two computations per call and its save-area cache never hits. In comparison.ts the astronomy-engine loop parses a Date string every iteration while the WASM loop calls swe_julday; deno_throughput.ts warms up only astronomy-engine. Swiss Ephemeris AGPL terms apply to anything distributing the WASM binary.

notes: Numbers verified on README; harness is public but lacks hardware/versions. Main shortcomings: wins only the Moon row (1.44x) and loses Sun rows ~1.8-2.4x; fopen stub means SEFLG_SWIEPH falls back to Moshier (no ephemeris files in WASM, rc_flags never checked); MIT label covers only the wrapper, bundled Swiss Ephemeris is AGPL-3.0/commercial.
